extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning calculus / real analysis
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of limits, continuity, monotone sequences, compactness, and fundamental theorems (Bolzano, Weierstrass) with epsilon-delta definitions and illustrative proofs for undergraduate-level real analysis/calculus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of monotone sequences (monotone convergence)
rubrics_metrics.description: A monotone increasing but bounded sequence of real numbers has a limit (converges).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof given by expressing terms as infinite decimals and showing that for each decimal place the digits stabilize after some index; equivalently provable from nested intervals or Dedekind cuts. Emphasizes that monotone bounded sequences often define numbers and are used to define sums/products of infinite decimals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of addition and multiplication of infinite decimals via monotone sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Given two positive infinite decimals a and b, form x_n by truncating each at n'th place, adding (or multiplying) the finite decimals; then the sequence x_n is monotone increasing and bounded, so define a + b = lim x_n (similarly for product).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoids attempting digitwise operations from the right (no right end). Example: adding 0.3333... and 0.989898... by truncation. Extensions by arithmetic rules handle sign cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Euler's number e as limit of partial sums
rubrics_metrics.description: Define a_n = 1 + 1/1! + 1/2! + ... + 1/n!; the sequence a_n is monotone increasing and bounded (e.g., by 3), so e = lim_{n->∞} a_n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternate expression as infinite series e = sum_{k=0}^∞ 1/k!; use bounding of tail to compute e to desired accuracy (error estimate by comparing remainder to geometric series).

rubrics_metrics.name: Computing limits/series to a given accuracy using remainder bounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Use estimates of the remainder (tail) of a convergent series to bound the error and determine how many terms are needed to obtain a given decimal accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: sum up to 1/12! gives e correct to nine digits; show remainder < desired epsilon by comparing to a geometric series or explicit inequalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof outline for irrationality of e
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume e = p/q, multiply the series expression of e by q! and show the fractional remainder is a positive number less than 1, contradicting integrality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiply by q! to isolate an integer part and a positive remainder bounded by a convergent geometric series sum < 1; conclude contradiction. Requires q ≥ 2 because 2 < e < 3.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of pi via limits of polygon perimeters
rubrics_metrics.description: Define circumference length (2π) as the limit of perimeters of inscribed and circumscribed regular n-sided polygons: p_n < 2π < q_n with p_n and q_n monotone sequences converging to 2π.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As n increases both sequences approach 2π monotonically; nested interval framework yields increasingly tight error margins for approximating 2π. Formulae with nested radicals provide concrete approximations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continued fraction representation and behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Finite continued fractions represent rational numbers; applying the Euclidean algorithm to irrationals yields infinite continued fractions whose convergents are rational approximations. Real quadratic irrationals have periodic continued fraction expansions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction via recursive substitution; examples include expansions for √2−1 and mention of continued fractions for e and π (Euler). Use as limiting processes of rational approximants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epsilon-delta definition of limit for functions (Cauchy's definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: The function f(x) has the limit a as x tends to Xi if, for every ε>0 there exists δ>0 (depending on ε) such that |f(x) − a| < ε for all x satisfying 0 < |x − Xi| < δ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy with sequential limit: replace 'sufficiently large n' by 'sufficiently near Xi'. Emphasizes exclusion of x = Xi in the definition, and the logical reversal of quantifiers (for every ε choose δ).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation and philosophical remarks on epsilon-delta limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The (ε,δ)-definition is static and does not presuppose motion; it makes 'continuous approach' a notion verifiable by observable conditions and resolves paradoxes like Zeno's by avoiding metaphysical motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlights that 'x tends to Xi' has no independent meaning outside the (ε,δ)-context and stresses practical verification: fix ε then find δ. Encourages constructing an explicit δ = φ(ε) in proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit of sin x / x as x → 0 (squeeze inequality approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: Show 1 < x/sin x < 1/cos x (for small x) and deduce sin x / x → 1 as x → 0; specifically derive inequality 1 − x^2/2 < cos x and hence bounds leading to |sin x / x − 1| < x^2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use geometric area comparisons on the unit circle: triangle, sector, triangle comparisons give sin x < x < tan x; divide and manipulate to obtain the sandwich inequalities. Works for x→0 from both sides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits as x → ∞ definition
rubrics_metrics.description: The function f(x) has limit a as x tends to infinity if for every ε>0 there exists K>0 (depending on ε) such that |f(x) − a| < ε whenever |x| > K (or x > K for one-sided limits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy to sequences (n→∞). Notes difference that x can go to +∞ or −∞ and defines one-sided limits X→+∞ or X→−∞.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precise definition of continuity at a point (epsilon-delta characterization)
rubrics_metrics.description: f(x) is continuous at x = Xi if the limit lim_{x→Xi} f(x) exists and equals f(Xi); equivalently for every ε>0 there exists δ>0 s.t. |x − Xi| < δ implies |f(x) − f(Xi)| < ε.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuity requires both existence of limit and equality to function value. Provides geometric band-picture (vertical band of width 2δ maps into horizontal band of width 2ε) and contract metaphor: for any ε you must produce a δ(ε).

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive method for proving continuity (explicit δ = φ(ε))
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove continuity at Xi, construct an explicit positive function δ = φ(ε) so that |x − Xi| < δ implies |f(x) − f(Xi)| < ε for every ε>0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: for f(x)=x^2 at Xi=0 one may take δ = sqrt(ε). Shows practical method used throughout to verify continuity of polynomials, rationals (away from poles), trig functions, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bolzano's Intermediate Value Theorem (root existence)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is continuous on closed interval [a,b] and f(a) < 0 < f(b) (or vice versa), then there exists c in (a,b) such that f(c) = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via successive bisection producing nested intervals whose intersection point exists by the Dedekind-Cantor postulate; continuity is used to derive contradiction if f at the limit point were nonzero. Emphasizes interval-halving (bisection) constructive method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weierstrass extreme value theorem (existence of maxima/minima)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is continuous on a closed interval [a,b], then f attains a greatest value M and a least value m at some points in [a,b].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof parallels Bolzano: bisect and select nested intervals narrowing to a point z where the max (or min) is achieved; continuity ensures contradiction if a larger value existed outside the nested intervals. Notes failure if function discontinuous or domain not closed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of nested intervals / Dedekind-Cantor postulate for existence proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Many existence theorems reduce to constructing nested closed intervals whose lengths shrink to 0; the Dedekind-Cantor postulate guarantees a common point in all intervals which is then shown (via continuity or other properties) to satisfy the desired condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied in Bolzano, Weierstrass, and monotone sequence convergence proofs; constructive bissection / interval selection procedures are typical applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compactness via sequential criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: A set S (in a metric/distance context) is compact if every sequence in S has a subsequence that converges to a limit element in S; closed intervals [a,b] are compact, while the whole real line and open intervals (0,1) are not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives examples (set of triangles with vertices in a disk is compact). Notes compactness generalizes closed bounded intervals and is used to extend Weierstrass' theorem to higher dimensions (closed domains).

rubrics_metrics.name: Excluding equality in limit definition when function undefined at the point
rubrics_metrics.description: In the limit definition one requires 0 < |x − Xi| < δ so that x is allowed to approach Xi without necessarily equalling Xi; this permits defining limits even where f(Xi) is undefined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains connection to sequence limits where one never substitutes n=∞ and gives examples like f(x)=(x^2+x)/x which has a limit as x→0 though undefined at 0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Squeeze/sandwich reasoning as a method for limit proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Derive bounds on a function between two functions with the same limit to conclude the middle function has that limit (e.g., sin x < x < tan x leads to sin x / x → 1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often uses geometric comparisons or algebraic inequalities; recommended when direct computation is difficult. Used explicitly in sin x / x example.
